report:
## Findings

The weight of high-quality evidence does **not** support the idea that hydroxychloroquine (HCQ) reduces COVID-19 mortality — in fact, the evidence points the other way.

**Large randomized trials:** The UK RECOVERY trial, one of the largest randomized platform trials (1,561 patients on HCQ vs. usual care), found no reduction in 28-day mortality; the HCQ arm was stopped early because it showed no benefit (NEJM, https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa2022926). The WHO Solidarity trial, involving thousands of hospitalized patients across many countries, similarly found HCQ produced "little or no reduction" in mortality compared to standard care and halted that arm (NEJM interim results, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7727327/; WHO Q&A, https://www.who.int/news-room/questions-and-answers/item/coronavirus-disease-covid-19-hydroxychloroquine).

**Meta-analyses:** A large international collaborative meta-analysis of randomized trials (Axfors et al., *Nature Communications*) pooling data from both hospitalized and outpatient studies found HCQ was associated with **increased** mortality, not decreased mortality, and chloroquine showed a similar trend (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-021-22446-z). Other systematic reviews (e.g., PMC8220439, PMC8013604) likewise concluded HCQ alone showed no mortality benefit, and combination with azithromycin was linked to higher mortality in some analyses.

**Outpatient/early treatment trials:** Trials in non-hospitalized patients (e.g., early COVID-19 outpatient RCTs) also failed to show mortality or hospitalization benefits.

## Conclusion

The current view is incorrect: robust randomized controlled trial evidence (RECOVERY, WHO Solidarity) and pooled meta-analyses consistently show hydroxychloroquine does **not** reduce, and may even slightly increase, COVID-19 mortality. Early positive signals came from small, low-quality, non-randomized studies that were not replicated in rigorous trials.
